ChipStain

Label-free nuclear staining from bright-field microscopy — with a calibrated map of where not to trust it.

5th Pazhou Algorithm Competition · Kaggle1 / 14
We are team Hack2Publish — Hamid, Esfer, Foysal and Kahakashan — and this is ChipStain. It predicts a nuclear stain from a plain bright-field image, and tells you where not to trust that prediction.
The problem2 / 14

Every nuclear read-out on a chip starts with a stain — and every stain has a cost

Fixed stains

End the experiment

DAPI after fixation gives one time-point per chip; a time course needs one chip per point.

Live DNA dyes

Perturb the cells

Repeated excitation is phototoxic; live DNA dyes damage DNA and slow the cell cycle.

Reporter lines

Rarely available

Engineering a nuclear reporter is impractical for primary and iPSC-derived tissue — such as neurons.

In-silico labeling predicts the stain from bright-field. But a point prediction never says when it is wrong.

ChipStain · Hack2PublishCell number · growth · viability · morphology · dose–response
On an organ-on-a-chip, cell counts, growth and viability all start from a nuclear stain. But fixation ends the experiment, live dyes harm the cells, and reporter lines are rare for stem-cell tissue. In-silico labeling predicts the stain — but never says when it is wrong.
Our question3 / 14

Can we predict the nuclear stain and say — per pixel and per frame — how much to trust it? And does that trust signal beat simple alternatives?

Model

Stain + uncertainty

A U-Net that predicts, for every pixel, the nuclear intensity μ and its uncertainty σ — stabilised with β-NLL and test-time augmentation.

Validation

Tested, not assumed

σ is compared with a matched control (same network, L1 loss) and with uncertainty-free proxies, checked for calibration, imaging shift, a biological read-out and neurons.

Tool

Open and reproducible

CPU inference, public data and weights, three training seeds, and one command that regenerates every result.

ChipStain · Hack2PublishImpact area named by the organisers: bright-field → fluorescence translation
So our question is: can we predict the stain and say, per pixel and per frame, how much to trust it — and does that signal beat simple alternatives?

ChipStain · Hack2PublishAll data public, CC BY 4.0 · no personal or clinical data
All data are public. We train on HeLa cells and test on a whole held-out well. We add a 60-hour time-lapse, stem-cell-derived neurons, and a competing segmentation model. Every model is trained three times — twenty-one runs.
Architecture · the model5 / 14

One network, two outputs: the stain μ and its uncertainty σ

ChipStain · Hack2Publish≈24 M parameters · PyTorch · segmentation_models_pytorch
The model is a U-Net with a ResNet-34 encoder. Its head predicts two maps: the stain, mu, and its log-variance, the learned uncertainty, trained with the beta-NLL loss. At inference we average eight rotated and flipped views and add their disagreement to the variance.
Architecture · the whole system6 / 14

From bright-field to a trusted biological read-out — and how we validate it

ChipStain · Hack2Publishgithub.com/hamidhosen42/AI4S-Open-Innovation-AI-for-Life-Science
The whole system: data feed the training runs; the model turns one image into a stain and an uncertainty map; downstream we count nuclei, flag unusual frames, and fit growth curves from trusted frames. Everything is validated, and one command regenerates every result.

The prediction fails — and this model's σ says so

Mean σ
0.08 → 0.33
the demo shows a warning
Honest caveat

Across three training runs, σ rose under blur in only 1 of 3 — the released one. σ is not a reliable drift alarm — a cheap input focus check is: the demo flags this image with it, and it catches 100 % of blurred images in every run.

ChipStain · Hack2PublishReleased checkpoint = seed 0 · blur is a crude stand-in for defocus
Blurred by one pixel, the prediction fails, and this model's uncertainty jumps from 0.08 to 0.33. But honestly, across three training runs sigma rose under blur only once — so it is not a drift alarm. What does catch it is a cheap check on the input itself: image sharpness. The demo runs it on every upload, and it flags every blurred image in every run.

ChipStain vs the matched control: the same ImageNet U-Net trained with L1 and the same 8× augmentation; means over 3 seeds. The cost: 11 % higher pixel error (MAE).

ChipStain · Hack2Publish95 % CIs from a bootstrap over seeds and fields
Over three runs on 125 test images, ChipStain matches the same ImageNet U-Net trained with an L1 loss and the same augmentation in correlation, 0.768 versus 0.768, at 11 percent higher pixel error. Its uncertainty ranks errors far better — 0.47 versus 0.32 — and is close to calibrated: the 95 percent interval covers 92 percent of pixels, while the control's spread must be scaled 18-fold.
Does σ add information?10 / 14

σ finds the errors better than anything you could compute without it

  • Errors sit on bright nuclei, so brightness and edge strength are honest rivals
  • Over the whole curve σ wins clearly: AUSE 0.177 vs 0.271 (edges) and 0.308 (brightness)
  • At a single 20 % cut-off the margin is small — we report both
ChipStain · Hack2PublishSparsification: remove the highest-score pixels first; lower curve = better
Errors sit on bright nuclei, so brightness and edges are honest rivals. Over the whole ranking curve sigma wins clearly; at a single cut-off the margin is small.

ChipStain · Hack2PublishData: R. Guiet, EPFL BIOP, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.6139958, CC BY 4.0
The biological payoff: on a 60-hour time-lapse, label-free counts give a doubling time of 24.9 hours against 23.9 from the real stain — without a single fluorescence exposure. A sigma frame gate cuts the error from 9.1 to 4.1 percent — mostly by sending failing fields to human review; on the same fields without the gate it is 5.8 percent.
Robustness and transfer12 / 14

New imaging and new cells: what holds, and what does not

Imaging shift · 3 seeds per model

σ for trust in distribution; an input check for drift

  • Added sensor noise raises σ in every model and seed
  • Blur or a new modality breaks every model; σ warns in only 1 of 3 ChipStain seeds
  • A cheap input check (focus + feature distance) flags 100 % of simulated-blur and phase-contrast images, every seed; cost: 16 % false alarms
Neural cultures · iPSC motor neurons

A small paired set adapts the model

  • No weight updates (scale and plane set on 2 labelled wells): Pearson r 0.59, but nuclei undercounted
  • Fine-tuned on one well: r 0.76; on 20 wells: 0.77 (one seed)
  • Before fine-tuning, σ stayed in the normal range — it did not warn
ChipStain · Hack2PublishNeurons: Christiansen et al., Cell 2018, CC BY 4.0 · dish, not chip
Outside the training data: added noise always raises sigma, but blur or a new modality breaks every model and sigma warns only sometimes. A cheap check on the input — image sharpness and distance from the training features — catches every one of those images in every run, at the cost of some false alarms on a new well. On stem-cell-derived neurons, fine-tuning on one well raises the correlation from 0.59 to 0.76.
Limits and positioning13 / 14

When to use ChipStain — and when not to

If you need…UseWhy
Only a nuclear countA direct bright-field segmenterCellpose: nuclei F1 0.831 vs ours 0.708
A stain-like image plus a trust signalChipStainIntensity, texture and morphology downstream, with calibrated σ and a frame gate
A new microscope, cell type or chipFine-tune, then recalibrate σOne paired well already helps; run the input check, because σ alone will not detect the shift
  • No organ-on-chip images were available — validation is in a plate and a dish
  • Per-nucleus σ is no better than a simple brightness rule; references are automatic labels
ChipStain · Hack2PublishFull limitations: technical report, section 7
Our limits: for a count alone, a dedicated segmenter is better — F1 0.831 versus 0.708. ChipStain is for when you need a stain-like image with a trust signal. And we had no organ-on-chip images.
